description: Я инженер из Бишкека: занимаюсь встраиваемой электроникой и ПО для умной инфраструктуры, от печатных плат и прошивок до веб-разработки. Мне интересно делать реальные устройства, которые работают в городе, и я могу закрыть в команде весь цикл от железа до интерфейса. Ищу людей с навыками в дизайне, маркетинге, аналитике или бизнесе, чтобы вместе довести проект до готового продукта.
summary:
Sixth Sense is a web jukebox that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into live sound and vibration, so people who cannot see a map can still explore it. The user chooses one of eight tracks (night lights, aerosols, lightning, ocean temperature, wind, forest height, CO₂, atmospheric river) and a place on Earth. A ring of sound then closes in on that place. Pitch gives direction (high is north, low is south), stereo gives east and west, and loudness and brightness give the value. The browser reads the pixels of NASA SVS frames and synthesizes every sound at the moment of listening, so nothing is pre-recorded. The same values can also drive phone vibration and game controller rumble.

This answers the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by pairing EIC visuals with real-time sonification, with accessibility as a core theme. It matters because Earth science reaches the public almost only as pictures, which leaves out the at least 2.2 billion people with a vision impairment (WHO). Sixth Sense needs no install or special hardware, and it works from the keyboard and with screen readers.
details:
What it does and how it works. Sixth Sense is a static website that works as an Earth jukebox. The user picks one of eight tracks, each built from a NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) visualization from the Earth Information Center collection, and a place on Earth. A ring of 16 voices, laid on the sphere with great-circle geometry, shrinks onto that place. Each voice averages the map values on its own arc 30 times a second. Direction sets pitch (a major pentatonic scale, so any combination sounds consonant) and stereo position: high notes are north, low are south, left ear is west, right ear is east. The value sets loudness and brightness, and the phenomenon sets the instrument: lightning cracks, dust rustles, smoke crackles, wind rushes. The scales are fixed, so the same sound always means the same pixel value. For globe videos with no flat map, a vertical “needle” of 12 voices reads the pixels passing under it. The scan ends with a spoken summary for screen readers.

Benefits and intended impact. Earth science reaches the public almost only as pictures, so people who cannot see get none of it. Sixth Sense gives the same visualizations hearing and touch (phone vibration on Android, controller rumble), and it runs in a browser with no install, account or special hardware. It is designed first for blind and low-vision users, and it also gives science-centre visitors and students a new way to notice patterns.

Tools. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript modules with no build step and no third-party libraries; Web Audio, Canvas 2D, Web Speech, Gamepad and Vibration APIs; Python, NumPy, Pillow and FFmpeg for media preparation; Node.js test runner (89 unit tests) plus headless-Chrome checks; Vercel hosting. We used Claude (Anthropic) through Claude Code to write code and draft documentation, under our direction. We chose the idea, datasets and sound rules, and we reviewed and tested the result. No AI-generated images, video or audio is used, and no machine learning runs in the product.

Creativity. A normal image sonification sweeps a line across the picture and gives only time order. We put the listener at the centre of a ring of sound, so the map becomes an audible compass that says where things are around a place you care about. Every sound can be traced back to a pixel.

What we considered. Accessibility came first: full keyboard control, a live region for screen readers, an accessibility menu, reduced motion, and AA contrast. We were open about limits. We sonify rendered visualizations, not calibrated measurements, and we label five tracks “Data-true” and three “Visual”. Haptics have been checked only in browser emulation, and we have not yet tested with blind users, so we report no results. An Arduino tactile controller is designed in the repository as future work, but the site does not use it.
